about.title: La Canada Flintridge Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Workplace injuries in La Canada Flintridge often happen away from a traditional office — on landscaping crews working the foothill terrain, delivery drivers navigating Foothill Boulevard and the I-210 corridor, or contractors on residential remodel jobs common to this area. Under California law, workers' compensation is generally your only path against your employer, no matter who caused the accident. But when a subcontractor, equipment manufacturer, property owner, or another driver contributed to your injury, a separate third-party claim may be possible alongside your comp benefits. Navigating both systems at once, while recovering and managing medical appointments, is a lot to handle alone. Our team reviews the details of your incident, explains your options in plain terms, and helps you understand deadlines that apply to your situation. Your initial consultation is free, and we work on contingency, so there's no upfront cost to get answers.

whyChoose.title: Why Talk to an Attorney About Your Workplace Injury

items.title: Comp Isn't Always the Whole Story
items.desc: Workers' compensation is usually your exclusive remedy against your employer, but a negligent third party like a subcontractor or equipment maker may still be liable. We can help identify whether a separate claim applies to your case.

items.title: Reporting Deadlines Matter
items.desc: California requires injured workers to report the incident to their employer within 30 days. Missing this window can complicate your comp claim, so getting guidance early matters.

items.title: Retaliation Is Illegal, But Workers Still Worry
items.desc: It's against California law for an employer to punish you for reporting a workplace injury or filing a claim. We can explain your protections if you're concerned about your job.

items.question: I was hurt doing landscaping work near the Angeles Crest Highway area for a subcontractor. Can I file a claim against them directly?
items.answer: Possibly. If the subcontractor was a separate entity from your direct employer and their negligence contributed to your injury, a third-party claim outside the workers' comp system may be available. This is different from a standard workers' comp claim against your own employer, and it carries its own two-year filing deadline. We can review the working relationship and help determine your options.

items.question: Does it matter that my injury happened while driving for work on I-210 instead of at a job site?
items.answer: Not necessarily. Injuries that happen while performing work duties, including driving between job locations on routes like the I-210 corridor, are generally still covered under California workers' compensation. If another driver caused the crash, that could also open the door to a separate third-party injury claim. Both angles are worth discussing with us.

items.question: My employer told me not to file a claim after my injury. What are my rights?
items.answer: California law prohibits employers from retaliating against workers for reporting an injury or pursuing a workers' compensation claim. If you've been pressured, threatened, or discouraged from filing, that itself may raise legal concerns separate from your injury claim. We can walk you through your rights and next steps at no cost to you.
